posts.title: India thought the protest was about education.
posts.author: Dr Deepessh Divaakaran Dr DD
posts.snippet:
India thought the protest was about education.
But the target was never Dharmendra Pradhan.
Or even Modi.

The real target was Amit Shah.

31 March 2026.
Amit Shah marked the Naxal deadline complete.

In 2014, 
India had 126 affected districts.
By March 2026, only two remained.

For decades, the Red Corridor was not only a war.
It was an economy.

Extortion.
Weapons.
Contracts.
Fear.

An ecosystem lived from the fire.
Then the fire was switched off.

Enemy Number One had been selected.

But another file was already open.

9 January 2026.
Shah announced a three-year war on drugs.

26 June 2026.
The doctrine entered the record.
Amit Shah gave clear Mandate to All agencies.

DETECT.
DISRUPT.
DESTROY.

Not merely the street peddler.
The manufacturer.
The transporter.
The financier.
The kingpin.
The political shield.

Now open the Punjab file.

Punjab shares 553 kilometres with Pakistan.
Beyond it lies the Golden Crescent corridor.

The Afghan ban changed production.
It did not erase trafficking routes.
It just shifted to Pakistan.

Packets now travel by drone.
By courier.
By cargo.
By encrypted instruction.

Money returns through hawala.
Crypto.
Property.
Front companies.

Punjab is not merely a consumer.

It is an entry gate.
A warehouse.
A redistribution point.
A pharmaceutical-diversion risk.

Punjab drug consumption:
~₹18,000 crore.

Transit and interstate distribution:
~₹30,000 crore.

Pharma diversion and synthetics:
~₹7,000 crore.

Total drug economy:
~₹55,000 crore.

That is ~₹150 crore every day.

No corridor this large survives on criminals alone.

It needs warnings.
Transfers.
Silence.
Weak prosecutions.
Protected routes.

A 3% protection rent means ₹1,350 crore.
At 5%, it becomes ₹2,250 crore.

Enough to feed Beuraucrats.
Brokers.
Gangsters.
Election machines.
Political Leaders.

And expensive silence.

Punjab votes soon.

A serious crackdown could destroy more than drugs.
It could destroy cash flows.
Protection networks.
And political futures.

Then came Jantar Mantar.
The banner said students.
The speeches named Pradhan.
The anger moved towards Modi.

But the loudest demand reached Amit Shah.
Now you know why Amit Shah was quiet over 50 days.

Intelligence does not begin with confession.
It begins with motive.

Timing.
Money.
And fear.

The protest may have ended.

The investigation has only begun.

posts.title: Vírus Ransomware
posts.author: Henrique Oliveira
posts.snippet:
Vírus Ransomware

Introdução

O ransomware é um tipo de malware (software malicioso) desenvolvido para impedir o acesso aos dados ou sistemas de um utilizador, normalmente através da encriptação dos ficheiros, exigindo o pagamento de um resgate (ransom) para restaurar o acesso. É uma das ameaças cibernéticas mais perigosas da atualidade, afetando pessoas, empresas, hospitais, escolas e entidades governamentais.

O que é um ransomware?

O ransomware é um programa malicioso que, após infetar um computador ou uma rede, bloqueia ou encripta ficheiros importantes. Em seguida, apresenta uma mensagem exigindo o pagamento de um resgate, geralmente em criptomoedas, prometendo fornecer uma chave de desencriptação.

Como o ransomware se propaga?

As formas mais comuns de infeção incluem:

E-mails de phishing com anexos ou ligações maliciosas;

Transferência de programas piratas ou ficheiros infetados;

Exploração de vulnerabilidades em sistemas operativos e aplicações desatualizadas;

Dispositivos USB infetados;

Sites comprometidos ou maliciosos.


Como funciona?

1. O utilizador abre um ficheiro ou ligação maliciosa.

2. O ransomware instala-se no sistema.

3. Os ficheiros são encriptados.

4. É apresentada uma nota de resgate com instruções de pagamento.

5. Mesmo após o pagamento, não existe garantia de recuperação dos dados.

Tipos de ransomware

Crypto-ransomware: encripta ficheiros e documentos.

Locker ransomware: bloqueia completamente o acesso ao dispositivo.

Scareware: apresenta falsas mensagens de infeção para enganar a vítima.

Double Extortion: além de encriptar os dados, os criminosos ameaçam divulgar informações confidenciais.

Exemplos de ransomware

WannaCry

Petya

NotPetya

Locky

Ryuk

Consequências

Perda de dados importantes;

Interrupção das atividades de empresas e instituições;

Prejuízos financeiros elevados;

Exposição de informações confidenciais;

Danos à reputação da organização.

Como prevenir ataques de ransomware?

Manter o sistema operativo e os programas atualizados;

Utilizar antivírus e firewall confiáveis;

Fazer cópias de segurança (backups) regularmente;

Não abrir anexos ou ligações de remetentes desconhecidos;

Utilizar palavras-passe fortes e autenticação multifator;

Formar os utilizadores sobre boas práticas de cibersegurança.

O que fazer em caso de infeção?

Desligar imediatamente o equipamento da rede.

Não pagar o resgate, pois isso não garante a recuperação dos dados.

Informar a equipa de informática ou segurança.

Restaurar os ficheiros a partir de backups seguros, quando disponíveis.

Analisar o sistema antes de o voltar a utilizar.

Conclusão

O ransomware representa uma das maiores ameaças à segurança da informação. A prevenção, a atualização constante dos sistemas, a realização de backups e a sensibilização dos utilizadores são as melhores formas de reduzir o risco de infeção e minimizar os impactos de um ataque. Conhecer o seu funcionamento é essencial para proteger dados e infraestruturas digitais.

⚡ Tolvira Threat Intel — Tuesday, July 28, 2026
━━ TODAY'S TOP THREATS ━━
🤖 SourTrade — Browser Builds Its Own Malware
 A malvertising operation makes victims' browsers assemble the final Windows executable themselves — using a legitimate runtime as its base. No complete malicious file served from a fixed URL. Operating since late 2024 across 12 countries, impersonating trading and crypto platforms. File-based AV and DLP miss it entirely. Behavioural EDR catches it.
🏟️ The Gentlemen Ransomware — Thialf Ice Rink Extortion
 The Gentlemen group is threatening to leak all stolen data from the Netherlands' premier speed skating venue unless ransom is paid within days. Cultural institutions and sports venues are soft targets — high reputational leverage, limited security budgets, NIS2 scope many don't expect to be in.
📱 Android Ad Fraud — After Every Call
 A new fraud trend is bombarding Android users with ads after every phone call. Mobile devices remain the least-governed endpoint in most enterprise environments. MDM enforcement and mobile threat defence are not optional when corporate data flows through employee handsets.
🔓 Anubis Group Claims New Breach — Leak Threatened
 Anubis cybercrime group claimed a new attack and is threatening to release stolen data. Ransom-driven extortion without encryption is now the dominant model — no operational disruption, maximum reputational leverage, minimum attacker footprint.
━━ CRITICAL CVEs ━━
🔴 CVE-2026-61511 | Deserialization | RCE — No Auth Required
 Critical unauthenticated RCE. No confirmed in-the-wild exploitation as of July 27 — but public PoC changes that status rapidly. Patch before the window closes.
🔴 Invisible Desktop MaaS | Windows | Covert Persistent Access
 MaaS operation launches legitimate browsers on an invisible desktop — giving attackers persistent remote access through processes that look normal. Hunt for browsers spawning from unusual parents and making outbound connections outside business hours.
🔴 SharkNinja Smart Vacuum | Unpatched IoT Spy Risk
 Unpatched flaw turns a vacuum cleaner into a surveillance device. IoT in corporate environments is the most consistently unmanaged attack surface. Separate network segment. Asset inventory. Non-negotiable.
━━ THREAT PATTERN ━━
This week's attacks hide inside legitimate tools. Legitimate runtime. Legitimate browser. Legitimate appliance. Detection that asks "does this look malicious?" fails here. Behavioural baselines, anomaly detection, and Zero Trust segmentation catch what signatures miss.

I almost fell for a dev job scam today. Got an offer for a $150/hr remote role and was asked to clone/run a private GitHub repo locally before a meeting. Thought it was too good to be true, and it definitely was.

🚨 ​Anatomy of a Billion-Euro Phantom Transfer❗⚠️The "CryptoHost API" Scam Exposed❗

⚠️ ​If someone hands you a document claiming to transfer €1 Billion directly into your bank account via a "CryptoHost Conversion" or "Smart Contract API"—
⚠️STOP❗ 
⚠️ It is a 100% fabricated advance-fee scam❗

⚠️ ​The image below is a real document being circulated in secondary project financing and commodity deals. 
⚠️ On the surface, it uses impressive tech-jargon: 
⚠️ Ethereum endpoints, Alchemy API keys, SWIFT TRNs, and Smart Contract Hashes❗

⚠️ ​When you conduct a forensic breakdown, the entire scheme falls apart in seconds:

🏦↔️⚡​The Fake SWIFT-to-Blockchain Bridge❗
⚠️​The Claim❗
👉 A SWIFT transfer (GB98765854358048) for €1,000,000,000 automatically converts into 1.16 Billion USDT via a "CryptoHost API"❗

⚠️​The Reality❗
👉 SWIFT is a closed, secure messaging network between licensed banking institutions❗
❌ SWIFT does not natively trigger public Ethereum node APIs to execute instant, off-ledger fiat-to-crypto settlements❗

⛓️​ Basic Blockchain Technical Contradictions❗

⚠️​Public Node Abuse❗
👉 The document lists an exposed Alchemy API endpoint (eth-mainnet.g.alchemy.com)❗ 
⚠️ Alchemy is simply a public node provider used by developers to query the blockchain
🅾️⚠️ It has zero authority to hold, convert, or credit banking funds❗

⚠️​Mislabeled Token Contract❗ 
👉 The "Token ID" listed (0xdAC17F958D2ee523a2206206994597C13D831ec7) is literally just the public smart contract address for USDT (Tether) on Ethereum. 
❌ It is not a unique security, private balance, or project asset

💻 ​The "API Screen Connection" Illusion❗
⚠️ ​The document references entering "Blocking and Release Codes into a Panel" to mirror funds into an "available balance without gas fees"❗
❌ ​There are no gas-free, download-free crypto injections into central bank accounts ⚠️ This illusion is created purely to convince victims that funds are "locked" and waiting to be released❗

🪤 ​How The Trap Works❗
⚠️ ​Once you accept this document as proof of funds, the fraudster will claim❗
⚠️​"The €1 Billion is ready in the cloud mirror account❗ 
👉 You just need to pay a $25,000 'gas fee', 'node activation fee', or 'server connection charge' to complete the release"
​⚠️ The scammer presents massive funding 1.16 B USDT using impressive-looking technical terminology (APIs, Smart Contracts, SWIFT TRNs, Session IDs).
⚠️ ​The Illusion❗ 
👉 They claim the file is "TOKENIZED" and requires no conversion, creating urgency for a "technician-to-technician" setup❗
⚠️ ​The Trap (The Advance Fee)❗ 
👉 Soon, the sender will claim that to "release" or "unblock" the transaction, a server key, gas fee, cloud registration fee, or mirror-account fee must be paid in advance. ⚠️ Once you pay, 
⚠️​Once that advance fee is paid, 
🛑 The scammer vanishes🚩
🛑They disappear❗

❌ ​Don't let pseudo-technical terminology blind your due diligence.

posts.title: I almost walked straight into a very well run scam this week. Sharing the full story because I think a lot of people in this space wouldn’t have caught it.
posts.author: Karim Mango
posts.snippet:
I almost walked straight into a very well run scam this week. Sharing the full story because I think a lot of people in this space wouldn’t have caught it.

I’ve been sourcing a 1MW hydro cooled container for a project, so I’ve been active in the market talking to vendors. A day after I started that search, I got a LinkedIn connection request from a “Tom Rubin,” 260 connections, 40 mutuals, claiming to be COO of BixBit. Nothing screamed fake. I even checked BixBit’s Twitter/X and found a real post referencing a “Tom Rubin” at the EIF conference. No photo attached, but the name checked out.

So I reached out about pricing on BixBit’s containers since they fit what I needed. He sent me a Calendly link that looked completely normal, and I booked a same day call.

First red flag: the calendar invite came back with no meeting link at all, and a strange reply to email address. I figured it was a glitch and just sent over my own Google Meet link to be safe.

When the meeting time came, “Tom” said he’d send the link shortly. What showed up was a broken, fake Microsoft Teams link, even though I had sent a Google Meet invite. I scanned it. Flagged as malicious. I told him it wasn’t working and that my antivirus wasn’t letting me open it. He regenerated a new “Teams” link. I scanned that one too, same result, flagged malicious.

I told him to just join my legitimate Google Meet instead. His response was to disable my antivirus and join, insisting people were waiting for me on the call. I said no and ended it there. He then asked me to screenshot the error, so I sent him the scan results showing the malicious flag. He blocked me within seconds.

This was a textbook credential harvesting and wallet draining setup. A real company impersonated, a name lifted from a legitimate conference mention, a clean Calendly funnel, and a fake meeting client designed to either phish credentials or push malware, all timed right after I started shopping the market. If I didn’t work in cybersecurity and hadn’t scanned that link myself, I could easily have fallen victim to this scam.

A few takeaways:
• Mutuals and a plausible backstory are not verification.
• Always verify meeting links independently, especially ones sent outside the platform you originally proposed.
• If someone pressures you to disable security software to join a call, that is the call.
• Screenshot it, report it, don’t just walk away quietly.

Screenshots attached below.

On an unrelated note, I am still genuinely looking for a legitimate 1MW hydro container, ideally already located in the US. If you’re a real vendor or know one, feel free to reach out.
#CyberSecurity #Scam #Crypto #InfoSec #DueDiligence #BitcoinMining

posts.snippet:
Putting payments leader, Amol Gharte, in the spotlight 💡

Amol has 10 years of experience in crypto and formerly ran large teams at Meta. Today, he's the Co-Founder of Solana Spaces

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗱𝗶𝗱 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗲𝗻𝗱 𝘂𝗽 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝗻 𝗽𝗮𝘆𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀?
I didn't start out chasing payments specifically. I've now spent a decade in crypto, ran large teams at Meta, did finance and VC work before that. When I left that world to go all-in on crypto I knew one thing: finance will change forever with crypto rails. Our business Solana Spaces touches payments to ingest customer payments to sell retail merchandise, and b2b partnership / consulting payments for events.

We used Stripe, Chase Bank and Zelle for payments prior to us establishing the onchain payment alternative simply because we kept hitting the same wall over and over: every commerce problem — vendor payouts, event ticketing, merch fulfillment, sponsorship transfers — came back to money moving too slowly or too expensively. Legacy rails charge fees and take days to settle.

We knew that once you're running a marketplace with vendors who need cash flow, that's not a footnote, it's the whole business. Solana's near-zero transaction costs turned payments from a cost center into the actual product wedge. By year end 2025 we did greater than 50% of total revenue, payments, transfers, payroll all onchain. It saved us days of transfer time and hundreds of dollars in transfers.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁'𝘀 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗮𝘀𝘀𝘂𝗺𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝗲𝘆 𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂'𝘃𝗲 𝗵𝗮𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝘂𝗻𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻?
That slow settlement equals safety. Coming out of Chase and Zelle and traditional banking rails, I'd absorbed this idea without even questioning it: if a payment takes days to clear, that's the system protecting you. Holds, pending states, net-30 terms, I treated all of it as trust infrastructure, not friction.
Running Solana Spaces broke that assumption fast. On our marketplace we route vendor payments through smart contract escrow with a three-tranche release, 30% when the order is confirmed, 40% when shipping is posted onchain, 30% on delivery. None of that trust comes from making anyone wait. It comes from the release conditions being enforced by code instead of a bank's internal process. We can verify exactly where a payment sits at any moment, and so can the vendor, and so can the buyer.

Once you can prove state onchain, speed and trust stop being the same variable. We moved over 50% of total revenue, payments, transfers, and payroll onchain by the end of 2025, and disputes didn't go up, they went down. The slowness was never protecting us. It was just the only tool centralized rails had.
P.S This isn't to say onchain payments don't need to work on scams, fraud, accidental transfers etc. that's a whole separate battle we have to keep fighting. Simply that onchain payments are better than offchain. Period.

Unfortunately, not everything in crypto can be considered a genuine investment. Due to the large number of scams and fake investment platforms, the crypto industry has unfairly gained a reputation for being risky and untrustworthy.

posts.title: I almost ran malware today.
posts.author: Dominik De-Sade
posts.snippet:
I almost ran malware today. 
It was disguised as a QA job assessment.
The approach was textbook-professional. 
A recruiter reached out on LinkedIn about a Web3 staking platform + 3D game. 
Real-sounding pitch, $5.2M seed funding, a proper JD in PDF, salary range, a 4-step hiring process. 
We negotiatedת Everything felt normal.
Then came the "30-minute assessment": a ZIP with the game's source code and a demo video, with instructions to run git checkout pixie-video to see the video.
That command is the payload. The ZIP ships with a pre-built .git folder containing malicious hooks - scripts git executes automatically on checkout. One innocent-looking command and an infostealer grabs your browser passwords, session cookies, and crypto wallets. There is no video. There is no job.
What saved me: I checked the file before running anything.
The red flags, in hindsight:
🚩 Delivery via a file-sharing link, not a company GitHub
🚩 "The video is in a git branch" - nobody stores videos in branches
🚩 LinkedIn itself flagged one of the messages as potentially harmful
🚩 Urgency: assessment sent minutes after I agreed
🚩 Web3 + remote + flexible hours + fast process = the perfect bait for our industry
How to protect yourself:
✅ Verify the person: verification badge on their profile (ID-verified), real company page, their name on the company website. Google "company name + scam"
✅ Check links BEFORE clicking: VirusTotal, urlscan.io
✅ Check files AFTER downloading, BEFORE opening: upload to VirusTotal or Hybrid Analysis
✅ Never run a recruiter's code on your main machine. VM or sandbox only - assume it's hostile until proven otherwise
✅ A ZIP containing a .git folder = never run git commands in it. Hooks execute arbitrary code
✅ Legit assessments live on public GitHub repos, TestGorilla, HackerRank - not in ZIPs from LimeWire
✅ Insist on a video call before doing any task. Scammers avoid faces
✅ Turn off "hide extensions" in your OS - "video.mp4.exe" still fools people
This pattern matches known fake-interview campaigns (some attributed to North Korean threat actors) specifically targeting Web3 and crypto professionals. If you work in this space, you ARE a target.
I reported the profile. If you got a similar "assessment" - don't run it, report it.
Stay paranoid. In QA, paranoia is a professional skill. 🛡️
P.S after I wrote last message, user were removed from Linkedin
#QA #CyberSecurity #Phishing #Web3 #JobScam #InfoSec #QALead

posts.title: Artificial intelligence is transforming the way we communicate—but unfortunately, it's also changing the way fraudsters target investors.
posts.author: Dereck Johns
posts.snippet:
Artificial intelligence is transforming the way we communicate—but unfortunately, it's also changing the way fraudsters target investors.
Deepfakes and AI-powered voice scams (often called vishing) are becoming increasingly sophisticated. Criminals can now create convincing videos of public figures promoting fake investment opportunities or clone the voice of a loved one or financial professional to pressure you into sending money or sharing sensitive information.

As a state securities regulator, we've seen firsthand that investment scams continue to evolve. While the technology changes, the warning signs often remain the same:
🔹 Pressure to act immediately
🔹 Promises of guaranteed or extraordinary returns
🔹 Requests to keep the conversation secret
🔹 Demands for personal information, passwords, or verification codes
🔹 Payment requests through wire transfers, gift cards, cryptocurrency, or payment apps

The best defense is to slow down and verify.
If you receive an unexpected call, text, or video involving your finances, hang up and contact your financial institution or investment professional using a trusted phone number—not the one provided in the message. A few extra minutes of verification can prevent a costly mistake.

Investor protection isn't just about enforcing securities laws—it's also about empowering investors with the knowledge to recognize fraud before it happens.

Take the time to talk with your family about these emerging scams, especially older adults who are often targeted. Awareness is one of the strongest tools we have in the fight against financial fraud.

posts.title: ₹30,000 became ₹89,96,873... on the screen.
posts.author: Kapil Banati
posts.snippet:
₹30,000 became ₹89,96,873... on the screen.
But when the investor tried to withdraw even ₹1, he was told to first pay "10% tax".
He paid.
The money still didn't come.
Then another demand followed.
Then another.
Only later did he realise that the entire "investment platform" never existed.
The profits were fake.
The trading dashboard was fake.
The advisors were fake.
The WhatsApp investment group was fake.
And his life savings had disappeared.
  

As a lawyer, I recently came across yet another FIR involving this exact modus operandi.
What is disturbing is not merely the amount involved—it is the professional sophistication of these cyber frauds.
The fraudsters don't hack your bank account.
They hack your trust.
Their script is almost identical every time:
✔ You are added to an "exclusive" WhatsApp stock market group.
✔ Daily messages show people making extraordinary profits.
✔ A friendly "investment advisor" gains your confidence.
✔ You are persuaded to download a professional-looking trading application.
✔ Initially, everything appears genuine. Your portfolio keeps growing. You feel you've discovered a golden opportunity.
Then comes the trap.
The moment you try to withdraw your money, you are asked to pay:
• Income Tax
• Security Deposit
• Unlocking Charges
• RBI/SEBI Compliance Fee
• Processing Charges
Every payment is described as "the final formality."
It never is.
The most dangerous aspect of these scams is that victims do not lose money because they are greedy.
They lose money because the fraudsters spend weeks or even months building credibility before stealing a single rupee.
That is social engineering at its most sophisticated.
Before you invest, remember:
🔹 Verify whether the broker or trading platform is genuinely registered with SEBI.
🔹 Never rely solely on WhatsApp or Telegram investment groups.
🔹 If an app shows huge profits but demands additional money before permitting withdrawal, consider it a glaring red flag.
🔹 No genuine investment platform asks you to deposit money merely to release your own funds.
As legal professionals, we are witnessing a worrying rise in such complaints.
Technology is advancing.
Unfortunately, so is financial crime.
Awareness is no longer optional—it is the strongest defence.

If this post prevents even one person from becoming the next victim, it will have served its purpose.

Please share it with your family, friends and colleagues. Someone in your network could be the next target.
#CyberCrime #InvestmentFraud #StockMarketScam #FinancialFraud #LegalAwareness #CyberLaw #SEBI #WhatsAppScam #ASKLEGAL

posts.title: A funding chain worth tracing: a consumer splits a purchase into four payments. The BNPL provider doesn't hold that credit, it warehouses and securitizes it. A share of the buyers
posts.author: Euron Porja
posts.snippet:
A funding chain worth tracing: a consumer splits a purchase into four payments. The BNPL provider doesn't hold that credit, it warehouses and securitizes it. A share of the buyers on the other end are private credit funds.
Total BNPL credit issuance across all product types is estimated at $150-160 billion in 2025 (Federal Reserve). Some of that gets packaged into asset-backed structures, with the riskier tranches held by private credit and insurance-affiliated buyers reaching for yield that corporate direct lending increasingly can't match.
What's missing from this picture is a reliable industry-wide number for private credit's aggregate exposure to BNPL warehouse lines. Individual facilities are disclosed, a purchase commitment in the hundreds of millions, recyclable into several times that in financed volume, but no one appears to publish the total.
That's not a footnote, it's the risk. A financing channel that isn't sized publicly is a financing channel that can tighten without warning. If funds under pressure elsewhere quietly pull back here, the first sign might just be that everyone's BNPL limit gets a little smaller, with no clear story about why.
posts.reason: Risk analysis of BNPL warehouse financing and private credit exposure is relevant to compliance and financial intelligence professionals, but focuses on traditional finance rather than blockchain or crypto.

comments.text: The absence of an aggregate exposure figure is itself informative — when individual warehouse facilities are disclosed but no one aggregates them, it usually means the risk is distributed across enough vehicles that no single regulator has a mandate to require the roll-up.
Do you see insurance-affiliated buyers marking these tranches differently than pure private credit funds, given their generally longer holding horizons and different liquidity pressures?
This mirrors what we see tracing structured flows more generally — the risk concealment isn't in any single facility's terms, it's in the fact that no one is required to publish the sum of the parts.

Digital Assets in Family Law: The Emerging Challenge of Cryptocurrency and Online Accounts in Property Equalization

As digital wealth proliferates, Ontario family law courts are grappling with novel valuation and disclosure challenges.

Key Issues at the Intersection of Digital Assets and Family Law:

1. Disclosure and Tracing
Cryptocurrency holdings (Bitcoin, Ethereum) and digital assets (NFTs, online business revenue streams) are often held pseudonymously across decentralized exchanges or self-custody wallets. Enforcement remains challenging.

2. Valuation Date Complexities
Digital assets are notoriously volatile. Ontario courts under the Family Law Act generally fix value as of the Valuation Date, but retain discretion to consider post-valuation date events.

3. Forensic Accounting
Courts are increasingly ordering forensic accounting reviews of digital wallets and exchange records.

4. Practical Strategies for Counsel:
- Include specific digital asset disclosure provisions in financial statements (Form 13.1)
- Request exchange records early in litigation
- Consider freezing orders where dissipation risk exists

posts.title: "Earn APY on carbon" was always a ponzi shape. Here's the mechanics, explained simply.
posts.author: KliSus
posts.snippet:
"Earn APY on carbon" was always a ponzi shape. Here's the mechanics, explained simply.
I want to explain why the carbon-crypto yield model was doomed — not as an insult, but as arithmetic. Once you see the shape, you can't unsee it, and you'll recognize it instantly the next time it appears wearing a different costume.
Start with a basic question you should ask of any yield: where does the money come from? A rental property pays yield from rent. A bond pays from interest. A SaaS dividend pays from customer revenue. In every legitimate case, the yield is downstream of someone paying for something real.
Now apply the question to carbon staking. KlimaDAO advertised yields that at times exceeded 35,000% APY, compounding every eight hours. Was there a flood of corporate buyers paying for carbon retirement, generating revenue to distribute? No. The yield was paid in newly minted KLIMA tokens. The protocol printed tokens and handed them to stakers.
That's the whole trick. Your "yield" was dilution. Every payout increased the supply, which meant every payout made each token worth less — unless new buyers arrived fast enough to absorb the new supply. Which means the returns of earlier participants depended entirely on the capital of later participants.
There's a name for that shape. It doesn't matter that nobody intended fraud, that the founders believed in the mission, or that the asset underneath was carbon rather than anything else. When yield comes from emissions instead of sales, the system requires exponential new demand to stand still. Exponential demand always stops. Then the math runs in reverse, at speed.
The tell, in every case, is the size of the number. Real verification work — satellites, audits, ratings — earns real margins: 20%, 40%, on a good day 80% gross. Nothing real pays 35,000%. The number wasn't the reward for the risk. The number was the risk.
At Klisus we sell verification, and our unit economics will be boring. Boring is the point. If anyone ever offers you yield on a climate asset, ask the one question that collapses the whole thing: paid from what?
Tomorrow's post: the one policy change that ended tokenized carbon overnight — and what it teaches about building on rules instead of around them.

posts.title: The domain is not the target. The deposit address is.
posts.author: LedgerCounsel
posts.snippet:
The domain is not the target. The deposit address is.

Another pirate IPTV network gets taken down. Domains seized, servers pulled, millions of subscribers. Days later it is back on a new domain.

The name changes. The hosting moves. The one thing that rarely changes is the payment wallet, because changing it means re-billing every customer mid-cycle.

That is the opening. Pull the crypto payment address off a few hundred of these storefronts, cluster by shared address, and thirty sites that looked like thirty operators collapse into one. The deposit wallet is the fingerprint the operator cannot rotate. Follow it forward and it ends at a regulated exchange that identified the account holder at onboarding.

That single move turns a takedown into a recovery: one named disclosure target instead of thirty anonymous domains, and it holds in an exhibit because the operator published the linking evidence themselves.

This is what we do. We start at the wallet, not the domain, and hand rights holders and their counsel a wallet-level exhibit pack sized to the disclosure instrument in their jurisdiction: the United Kingdom, European Union member states, the United States or Canada.

If you are running an infringement matter where the money moves in crypto, that is the part we can carry.

comments.text: The clustering step is the part most disclosure requests skip. Once you've got the shared deposit address, heuristic clustering across the exchange's own onboarding data usually turns up not just the operator but a handful of associated accounts opened with the same documents, which is often what actually moves a case forward.

How do you handle cases where the operator uses a payment processor or aggregator sitting in front of the wallet, so the on-chain trail ends at a custodial pooled address rather than an individually-KYC'd account?

We see the same pattern outside piracy: fraud storefronts rotate domains weekly but keep the same deposit wallet for months, because re-onboarding customers to a new address is operationally painful. That inertia is consistently the best lead in the file.

posts.title: CYBER NEWS: A Scattered Spider member pleaded guilty to an $8 million crypto theft built on SIM swaps
posts.author: Syba
posts.snippet:
CYBER NEWS: A Scattered Spider member pleaded guilty to an $8 million crypto theft built on SIM swaps

There's nothing clever in the method, which is why it keeps working. The crew sent text-message phishing to staff at large companies and collected logins. Then they called mobile carriers and talked a support rep into moving a target's phone number onto a SIM card they controlled. With the number in hand, every one-time code arrived on their phone, and they reset the accounts holding the cryptocurrency.

What makes this file worth reading is that it doesn't stay digital. A rival crew invaded the defendant's own home, assaulted his mother and threatened him with a blowtorch for his wallet keys. Investigators also pulled seed phrases belonging to his victims off a device in his house. A family's recovery phrase can sit in a stranger's evidence bag long before a single coin moves.

The coverage question: does the personal cyber policy pay for cryptocurrency taken through an account takeover the mobile carrier enabled, and is there any recovery against the carrier? Both are often excluded, sublimited, or fact-dependent, and carrier terms of service are usually written so you won't get far with the second one.

The control I'd want in place first: move every family member off SMS one-time codes to hardware security keys, then add a port-out PIN and a no-port note to every line. Every line means household staff and adult children, not just the principal, because the attacker picks whichever line is easiest.

Source: KrebsOnSecurity
posts.reason: Detailed breakdown of SIM-swap attacks and seed-phrase theft with insurance and carrier-liability analysis highly relevant to our CISO, insurer, and legal audiences.

comments.text: The insurance question is the right one to press, but there's a second layer worth flagging: even where a policy does pay out, subrogation against the carrier rarely succeeds because most carrier ToS disclaim liability for social-engineered port-outs, so the loss usually sits with the insurer or the victim regardless of fault.

Have you seen carriers actually enforce port-out PINs consistently at the support-rep level, or does the same social-engineering script that works on account resets also talk reps past the PIN requirement?

In tracing work after SIM-swap thefts, the funds are usually gone from the initial wallet within minutes, layered through several hops before the victim even notices the SMS codes stopped arriving. The hardware key recommendation is the single control we'd want in place before, not after, because there is rarely a fast enough window to act once the swap happens.

Nobody talks about drift until patch night fails.

A RHEL fleet doesn’t break all at once. It gets weird slowly: one repo changed, one crypto policy missed, one sysctl edited during a 2 AM incident. Across 400 nodes, that becomes uptime risk, failed OpenSCAP checks, and app teams blaming “Linux.”

We’ve been testing a self-healing pattern:

• Pull drift signals from Red Hat Insights, OpenSCAP, and Ansible facts  
• Compare against a RHEL 9.3 baseline by role, not by hostname  
• Use LangGraph agents to rank risk and draft remediation plans  
• Keep Ansible 2.16 as the only enforcement layer  
• Require approval for high-risk changes like kernel, auth, or crypto policy updates  

Before: manual troubleshooting across hundreds of nodes.

After: automated drift detection and remediation with 50-70% faster incident resolution.

Would you trust an AI agent to recommend remediations if Ansible remained the enforcement layer?

posts.title: $1.1 billion lost across 212 crypto exploits in H1 2026 the highest incident count on record. But the breakdown matters more than the total.
posts.author: Jaypalsinh Jadeja
posts.snippet:
$1.1 billion lost across 212 crypto exploits in H1 2026 the highest incident count on record. But the breakdown matters more than the total.

Smart contract vulnerabilities were the most common attack type. Yet they accounted for only 26% of losses. 

The real damage came from OpSec failures: compromised keys, signer compromises, bridge misconfigurations, backend breaches. Just those alone cost $789 million 74% of the total.

The KelpDAO attack (April, $292M) wasn't a code bug. Attackers compromised RPC nodes feeding a single-verifier bridge, forged a cross-chain message, and drained the contract. 

Drift Protocol ($285M, same month) used six months of social engineering to compromise multisig signers, then created a fake token with manipulated oracles and drained vaults in 12 minutes.

Two incidents. $577 million. Both could have been partially prevented with redundant verifiers, hardware wallet signers, and monitoring that catches anomalous activity.

The security frontier for protocols has moved from audits to infrastructure. Code reviews catch most vulnerabilities. Operational security stops the attacks that cost the most.

If you're building on-chain infrastructure, here's what matters: multi-verifier bridge setups, no pre-signed transactions without safeguards, hardware wallets for signers, real-time monitoring, incident response tooling.
posts.reason: Technical breakdown of OpSec failures in major bridge and protocol exploits with infrastructure lessons—directly valuable for security teams and potential incident clients.

comments.text: The distinction you draw is the one most risk teams still miss: audits reduce code risk, not operational risk. In our forensic work, the multi-verifier bridge point is key - a single-verifier design is a single point of failure disguised as infrastructure, not a smart contract issue at all.

On the Drift case - six months of social engineering before the multisig was compromised - did the monitoring stack have any anomaly detection on signer behaviour, or was it purely transaction-level? That gap seems to be where most of these OpSec failures actually live.

We consistently see the same pattern when tracing post-incident: the technical root cause is rarely the bottleneck for recovery, speed is. By the time a bridge misconfiguration or signer compromise is confirmed internally, funds are often already several hops into layering.

posts.title: When funds are stolen and moved through cryptocurrency, the investigation starts with what is already visible.
posts.author: Pinnacle Blocks
posts.snippet:
When funds are stolen and moved through cryptocurrency, the investigation starts with what is already visible.

Bank records require a court order, a cooperative institution, and time. Blockchain records require neither. Every transaction is public, permanent, and available from the moment it is written. That asymmetry matters enormously in the first hours after a theft.

Mixers and layering techniques complicate the picture, but they do not erase it. On-chain tracing follows value through obfuscation by analysing transaction patterns, cluster behaviour, and timing. The path may be indirect. It is rarely invisible.

What tracing cannot recover is time. The further funds travel from the point of theft, the closer they get to an off-ramp where they become considerably harder to freeze or seize. Early engagement preserves the evidential chain and keeps enforcement options open.

Blockchain forensics does not replace legal process. It informs it, and often makes it possible in the first place.

If you are looking at a situation involving missing digital assets, the first question is usually not whether there is a trail. It is how much of it remains actionable.

#BlockchainForensics #DigitalAssetInvestigation #CryptocurrencyTracing
posts.reason: Substantive educational post on blockchain tracing, mixer analysis, and timing of asset recovery directly targets lawyers and law enforcement investigating crypto theft.

comments.text: The asymmetry you describe cuts both ways though - public and permanent also means attackers know exactly what's visible, which is why layering through mixers and cross-chain swaps has become almost automatic in the first hour, not a later evasion step.

In your experience, at what point does the 'actionable' trail typically go cold - is it usually the first centralised off-ramp, or does cooperation from that exchange still leave a workable window afterward?

We tell clients the same thing about timing: the forensic trail rarely disappears, but the legal options attached to it - freezing orders, exchange holds - shrink fast, often within the first 24 to 48 hours.

posts.title: Digital anonymity is not a shield; it is a delay.

Digital anonymity is not a shield; it is a delay.

The FBI’s recent identification of a major Steam malware financier proves that even the most "private" ecosystems have physical and digital anchors.

How does a sophisticated malware operation collapse?

It started with a Google cookie.
It continued with 500 food deliveries.
It concluded with a Monero seed phrase.

The investigation into a malware campaign targeting Steam users demonstrates the power of multi-vector forensics. Investigators didn’t just follow the money: they followed the habits. By correlating over 500 Uber Eats orders with IP logs and persistent Google cookies, federal agents bridged the gap between a digital alias and a physical doorstep.

The better question for any organization isn’t whether your assets are on a privacy-focused blockchain, but whether your digital life is truly siloed.

Can you truly separate your personal digital footprint from your professional financial activity?
Is the perceived privacy of a seed phrase enough to offset the visibility of your daily habits?

At StonePath Investigations, we understand that blockchain tracing is only one piece of the puzzle. Effective asset recovery and fraud detection require a holistic view of the adversary’s behavior: from wallet flows to digital breadcrumbs.

In a world where every "private" transaction leaves a trail, expert analysis is the only way to find the truth.

Five years ago, more than 500 scientists and economists warned that climate policies treating biomass as a carbon-neutral energy source "create a model that encourages tropical countries to cut more of their forests", a warning the report said is now being borne out in Indonesia.

Earth Insight has called for the threat posed by the international trade in wood pellets to be included in International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) species assessments and Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species regulations. posts.title: A nice reminder from Justice Luc Morin that tax debts are not secondary debts, to be easily cast aside in an insolvency filing:
posts.author: Mark Taggart
posts.snippet:
A nice reminder from Justice Luc Morin that tax debts are not secondary debts, to be easily cast aside in an insolvency filing: 

[79] A tax debtor who fails to meet his fair share of his economic-social obligations by failing to pay his taxes is not merely evading the obligations of his social contract. Rather, in doing so, he is simply shifting the tax burden onto the shoulders of others whose burden is increased by the same amount. The defaulting tax debtor continues to benefit from the services associated with paying taxes, at the expense of an increased tax burden on his neighbours
. . .
[126] The deceased Bankrupt and his executor benefited from community-funded services: they travelled on public roads, benefited from municipal services, saw their children attend schools, and received care from dedicated medical professionals

[127] While our social safety net allows a citizen who has been affected by the vagaries of life to benefit temporarily from a respite when his or her financial means are insufficient, this benevolence cannot be equated with an invitation to avoid tax obligations or with a trivialization of evasions . . . 

Syndic de Le, 2026 QCCS 2751 (Que. S.C.), https://canlii.ca/t/km87s at paras 75-84, 125-130 [unofficial translation] 

Registrar Funduk made similar statements a quarter century earlier, but with his signature bluntness:

[13] The bankrupt enjoys the considerable benefits of being a Canadian citizen and an Alberta resident. Those benefits are not cost free. Taxpayers who do not pay their proper amount of tax are pickpockets. They pick the pockets of those taxpayers who do pay their taxes. What is so special about the bankrupt that paying taxpayers must bear a greater tax burden so he does not have to pay his proper tax liability? Canada has a substantial accumulated debt and each year pays substantial interest on that debt. Why should the bankrupt have a free ride, not once but twice.

[14] The trustee says that the bankrupt is slotted for a heart transplant. Will the bankrupt pay for that, or will the cost be borne by health care which is funded from public funds, which includes income tax? Why should paying taxpayers pay for the bankrupt’s heart transplant when he has twice now picked their pockets?

[15] A bankrupt who does not pay his taxes is not an honest and unfortunate debtor. He is one who takes advantage of the fact that his taxes are not collected by “source” deductions. This is misconduct.

[16] Rehabilitation is not the driving fact here. Deterence is, not just for the bankrupt but more important for others who might be tempted to evade income tax liability by conveniently using bankruptcy as a financial planning tool.

Re Trueman, 2001 ABQB 377 (Alta. Q.B.) <https://canlii.ca/t/5m7g>

posts.author: Immigria Consulting Firm
posts.snippet:
IRCC has updated its internal guidance on how immigration officers assess proof of funds for study permit applications.

The updated instructions, published on July 24, 2026, provide more detail on how officers should evaluate an applicant’s financial capacity. These instructions are used by IRCC staff when reviewing study permit applications and extensions.

Under the updated guidance, officers should assess more than the final balance shown in a bank account. They may consider:
• The amount and source of the funds
• Whether the funds are genuinely available to the applicant
• The history of the money in the account
• The financial and employment circumstances of the applicant or their family
• The probability that funding will remain available for future years of study
• Financial support from scholarships, relatives or other institutions

IRCC also lists bank statements covering the past six months as a common form of proof of funds. Depending on the circumstances, officers may request more extensive banking, employment or financial documentation.

Applicants must still demonstrate sufficient funds for first-year tuition, living expenses and transportation without relying on employment in Canada. Study permit extension applications must also meet the financial requirement again.

This update does not announce a new minimum proof-of-funds amount. Instead, it provides officers with more detailed guidance on how the source, availability and credibility of the funds should be assessed.

A strong study permit application should not only show enough money. It should clearly explain where the funds came from and demonstrate that they are genuinely available.

posts.title: She started the nonprofit to serve people, not to run an accounting system. So for a while, she tried to handle all of it herself.
posts.author: Nyquaise Moteng, CPA, EA
posts.snippet:
She started the nonprofit to serve people, not to run an accounting system. So for a while, she tried to handle all of it herself.

By the time she reached out to me, she was close to shutting down the organization.

The books did not reflect how the organization actually operated.

Grant funds and donations were not recorded in a way that showed how the money had been used. The accounting system had never been structured around the organization’s programs and funding sources.

Then came the larger problem.

After the organization failed to file its required Form 990-series return for three consecutive years, the IRS automatically revoked its tax-exempt status.

For a nonprofit that depends on grants and donations, that is not simply a paperwork problem.

It can affect funding, donor confidence, tax-deductible contributions, and the organization’s ability to continue operating.

The compliance problems had piled up to the point that closing felt easier than fixing them.

I am not sharing this to make anyone feel exposed.

Many nonprofit founders start the same way. They focus on serving people and believe they can shoulder the financial responsibilities themselves until the weight becomes too much.

Here is what we did.

We rebuilt the accounting system to reflect how the organization actually operates.

We organized transactions by program and funding source so that restricted funds could be traced to their use.

We corrected how grants and donations were recorded.

We addressed the outstanding filing requirements and began working through the process of reinstating the organization’s tax-exempt status.

The doors are still open.

She now has financial records she can stand behind and a path toward returning the organization to good standing.

This is the part of nonprofit work I want to talk about more here.

Not only the audit itself, but the quieter reality that many founders are trying to build something good while drowning in a financial system no one trained them to manage.

Asking for help is not failure.

Sometimes it is what saves the organization.

If the financial side of your nonprofit has gotten away from you, address it before the problem becomes a decision about whether to keep going.

That conversation is worth having early.

· EDR: حلول تراقب الأجهزة الطرفية، وتكتشف الهجمات، وتستجيب لها تلقائياً.
· XDR: نسخة متطورة من EDR تجمع وتحلل البيانات من مصادر متعددة (الأجهزة، الشبكات، البريد الإلكتروني، السحابة).
· SIEM: منصة لتجميع وتحليل سجلات الأحداث (Logs) بهدف اكتشاف التهديدات.
· SOAR: أدوات لأتمتة عمليات الاستجابة للحوادث، مما يقلل التدخل البشري ويسرع الاستجابة.
· Sandboxing: تشغيل الملفات المشبوهة في بيئة معزولة وآمنة لاختبار سلوكها.

ثالثاً: استخبارات التهديدات والصيد الاستباقي

· Threat Intelligence: معلومات وتحليلات عن المهاجمين، تكتيكاتهم، وأحدث التهديدات.
· Threat Hunting: عملية بحث استباقي ومنهجي عن تهديدات مخفية داخل الشبكة.
· IOC: مؤشرات مادية تدل على تعرض نظام أو شبكة للاختراق.
· IOA: سلوكيات وأنشطة تشير إلى وقوع هجوم، حتى قبل نجاحه.

رابعاً: أطر العمل وتكتيكات المهاجمين

· MITRE ATT&CK: إطار عمل عالمي يوثق تكتيكات وتقنيات المهاجمين وإجراءاتهم.
· TTPs: اختصار لأساليب وتقنيات وإجراءات المهاجمين.
· Exploit: برمجية أو تقنية تستغل ثغرة أمنية محددة.
· Zero-Day: ثغرة أمنية لم يُصدر لها المطور تحديثاً بعد.

خامساً: أنماط الهجمات والتهديدات الشائعة

· Ransomware: برمجية خبيثة تشفر الملفات وتطلب فدية لفك التشفير.
· Double Extortion: أسلوب يضيف تهديد نشر البيانات المسروقة إذا لم تُدفع الفدية.
· Phishing: رسائل احتيالية تهدف لسرقة بيانات حساسة.
· Spear Phishing: هجوم تصيد موجه ضد شخص أو مؤسسة معينة.
· Whaling: تصيد يستهدف كبار المديرين والمناصب القيادية.
· BEC: اختراق البريد الإلكتروني للشركات بهدف الاحتيال المالي.
· Supply Chain Attack: اختراق مؤسسة عبر استهداف مورد أو برنامج موثوق.
· Living Off The Land (LOTL): استخدام أدوات النظام الشرعية لتنفيذ الهجوم دون ترك برمجيات خبيثة واضحة.

سادساً: مراحل الهجوم والحراك الداخلي

· Privilege Escalation: رفع صلاحيات المستخدم للوصول إلى موارد حساسة.
· Lateral Movement: تنقل المهاجم بين الأجهزة داخل الشبكة بعد الاختراق الأولي.
· Data Exfiltration: سرقة أو نقل البيانات خارج المؤسسة.

سابعاً: إدارة الثغرات والتعاون الفريقي

· Patch Management: عملية إدارة وتثبيت التحديثات الأمنية بشكل منهجي.
· Purple Team: نموذج تعاوني بين الفريق الأحمر (الهجومي) والأزرق (الدفاعي) لتحسين الدفاعات بشكل مستمر.

posts.author: Abdu Samad NT
posts.snippet:
The ransomware group ShinHunters claims it breached Ernst and Young and says it plans to leak the allegedly stolen information if its demands are not met. While the claims are yet to be independently verified this reflects a growing trend where cybercriminals increasingly use public pressure and data exposure as part of their strategy rather than relying only on encryption.

For global organisations the biggest lesson is that cybersecurity is now a business resilience issue rather than only an IT responsibility. Strong security controls rapid incident response transparent communication and continuous monitoring are becoming essential as attacks grow more sophisticated. Whether or not every claim made by threat actors proves true every incident is a reminder that trust takes years to build and only moments to challenge.

#CyberSecurity #SecurityAffairs #ErnstAndYoung #EY #Ransomware #DataBreach #ThreatIntelligence #InformationSecurity #CyberDefense #RiskManagement #DigitalTrust #CyberResilience #InfoSec #Technology #BusinessSecurity
posts.reason: A substantive discussion of ransomware as business resilience by a security professional that would resonate with CISOs and compliance officers considering our NIS2/DORA incident response and crisis communications services.

comments.text: The shift toward extortion-by-exposure rather than pure encryption changes the incident response calculus: legal and comms teams need to be in the room from hour one, not brought in after containment. It also means data exfiltration timelines, not just encryption timestamps, become the critical forensic artefact.

Independent verification is the key phrase here - has anyone seen confirmation beyond the group's own claims, or are we still in the 'threat actor says so' stage that so many of these leak-site claims never move past?

We see this pattern often in ransomware-linked cases we're brought into: the extortion demand and the actual scope of compromise diverge significantly once the forensic picture is complete, which is exactly why premature public statements from either side tend to age badly.

posts.title: A sua empresa investiu milhões no perímetro, mas o atacante acabou de entrar usando a porta da frente. Com a chave de casa. 🔑💥
posts.author: Marcelo A.
posts.snippet:
A sua empresa investiu milhões no perímetro, mas o atacante acabou de entrar usando a porta da frente. Com a chave de casa. 🔑💥

O relatório mais recente sobre o cenário de ameaças na América Latina escancara uma realidade desconfortável: o Brasil continua liderando o volume de ataques de ransomware na região, e a tática dos grupos mais agressivos mudou drasticamente.
Eles não estão mais perdendo tempo tentando infectar o notebook do estagiário. 

O foco agora é:
1. Comprar ou roubar credenciais válidas (via Infostealers ou bots massivos de Credential Stuffing).
2. Entrar pela API ou portal de login sem acionar o WAF (afinal, a chave parecia legítima).
3. Mover-se lateralmente em minutos até o hipervisor de virtualização (VMware/Hyper-V) e destruir a infraestrutura de backups antes de rodar a criptografia.

Se a sua arquitetura de segurança ainda confia que "quem está dentro da rede é seguro", tenho uma má notícia: você não tem uma estratégia de contenção, tem apenas uma torcida.
A pergunta que os CISOs e lideranças de TI precisam responder hoje é: Se uma credencial corporativa for comprometida na próxima hora, o que impede essa pessoa de alcançar seu banco de dados crítico?
Se a resposta for "o firewall de borda", o estrago já está feito.

A contenção real exige duas coisas inegociáveis:
 Visibilidade e Mitigação de Bots/APIs na borda, eliminando o tráfego automatizado e descobrindo Shadow APIs antes que virem porta de entrada.
 Microsegmentação Zero Trust (Leste-Oeste), garantindo que mesmo se um invasor passar pela porta, ele fique preso dentro de um cômodo isolado sem conseguir mover um único byte para o resto do Datacenter.

Segurança moderna não é sobre tentar ser "impenetrável". É sobre ser incrivelmente resiliente quando o inevitável acontecer.

Como a sua infraestrutura está preparada para barrar a movimentação lateral hoje? 👇

#Cybersecurity #Ransomware #ZeroTrust #Microsegmentation #APISecurity #Akamai #InfoSec #CTO #CISO
posts.reason: A detailed technical analysis of modern ransomware tactics and Zero Trust containment by someone clearly addressing CISOs and IT leaders—exactly our target buyer personas for forensics and resilience services.

comments.text: Um ponto que costuma ficar de fora dessas análises: a velocidade com que o grupo destrói os backups antes de rodar a criptografia é frequentemente o momento em que a resposta ainda poderia ter mudado o desfecho, mas raramente há visibilidade suficiente para detectar isso a tempo no hipervisor.

Nos casos que você tem acompanhado no Brasil, a movimentação lateral até o VMware/Hyper-V geralmente acontece em minutos mesmo em ambientes com microsegmentação parcial, ou esse tempo cai drasticamente quando ela está bem implementada?

Em investigações de incidentes de ransomware que já analisamos, a credencial comprometida quase sempre já estava circulando há semanas antes do ataque - o problema raramente é a intrusão em si, é o tempo que ela passa despercebida.

posts.reason: A relevant article share on ransomware vulnerability management, but shallow engagement that adds little beyond the quoted material and provides limited opportunity to position our forensic and recovery expertise.

comments.text: Exposure management addresses the entry point, but the negotiation dilemma Ars Technica describes usually hinges on a separate question: whether the organisation can even establish, with evidence, what was actually taken versus what the attacker claims was taken.

Millard's point about known vulnerabilities and exposed systems is compelling - do you think the 'pay or not' decision would look different in organisations if they had accurate visibility into exfiltrated data before negotiating, rather than relying on the attacker's own claims?

In the cases we've been involved with, the pressure to pay quickly almost always outpaces the forensic clarity available at that point, which is precisely when decisions get made on incomplete information.
